extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media researchers, policymakers, and the general public interested in the state of journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative dimensions and metrics used to assess the health, practices, and performance of U.S. news organizations and journalists based on a large-scale survey of working journalists. Covers professional norms, newsroom conditions, audience relations, misinformation, diversity, and economic indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Job satisfaction and fulfillment
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of journalists' personal satisfaction with their jobs, excitement about their work, pride in their work, and whether they would choose the career again, as well as perceived impact on emotional well-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: ~70% say they are very or somewhat satisfied and often feel excited; large majorities are extremely or very proud; ~77% would choose their career again; about half say their job has a positive impact on emotional well-being (higher than the 34% who say it is bad). Used to evaluate individual and occupational morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern about future restrictions on press freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which journalists are worried about the prospect of press restrictions being imposed in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey finding: 57% are 'extremely' or 'very' concerned. Used to assess perceived threat to core democratic liberties and potential external risks to journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of misinformation and ability to recognize it
rubrics_metrics.description: How often journalists encounter made-up news and false information in their work and their self-reported confidence in recognizing misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: 71% say made-up news is a very big problem for the country; a large majority come across misinformation at least sometimes; most are confident in their ability to recognize it, but 26% of reporting journalists say they have unknowingly reported on a story later found to contain false information. This dimension also covers organizational capacity to manage/correct misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: News organizations' management/correction of misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of whether news organizations are doing a good job identifying, managing, or correcting misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About four-in-ten journalists say news organizations are doing a bad job managing or correcting misinformation. This metric assesses institutional practices and responsiveness to factual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to reporting false statements by public figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether journalists believe the best approach is to report on false statements so the public knows about them or to avoid reporting to deny attention to the falsehoods/public figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey finding: 64% favor reporting on the statement to inform the public; 32% favor not reporting to avoid amplifying falsehoods. This is a normative criterion for editorial decision-making about coverage of misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm of equal coverage (bothsidesism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether journalists think every side always deserves equal coverage in reporting or whether equal attention is not always warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey finding: 55% say every side does not always deserve equal coverage, while 44% say journalists should always strive to give every side equal coverage. This informs standards on balance vs. accuracy/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping journalists' own views out of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The norm that journalists should avoid inserting their personal views into their reporting, and assessments of whether journalists meet this standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: 82% say journalists should keep their views out of reporting; 55% think journalists largely are able to do this, while 43% say journalists are often unable. Used to evaluate impartiality and professional ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political leaning of audiences and political sorting
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the ideological composition of news audiences (left, right, mixed) and concern about political sorting—people getting news from outlets that share their views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists report audience leanings (32% left, 20% right, ~33% mixed); 75% say political sorting is a major problem, compared with 39% of the public. This dimension gauges perceived audience homogeneity and its effects on public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived possibility of universally accepted accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether journalists think it is possible to report news that 'nearly everyone finds accurate' and the degree of consensus on basic facts among journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: Three-quarters say journalists largely agree on basic facts; 52% say it's not possible to report news that nearly everyone finds accurate (public: 62%). This metric relates to credibility and the limits of universal agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public trust in news organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' perceptions of how much the public trusts information from news organizations, compared with the public's self-reported trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists' estimate: 14% think the public has a great deal or fair amount of trust; public survey: 29% of adults say they have at least a fair amount of trust. Used to evaluate perceived legitimacy and gaps between journalists' and public views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covering the most important stories of the day (core function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how well news organizations cover the most important stories of the day, one of five core journalistic functions evaluated in the report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists generally rate news organizations more positively than the public on this item. This dimension is used to judge editorial priorities and agenda-setting effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting the news accurately (core function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of news organizations' accuracy in reporting, another of the five core functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey example: 65% of journalists say news organizations do a very or somewhat good job reporting the news accurately, compared with 35% of the public. This directly measures perceived factual reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serving as a watchdog over elected leaders (core function)
rubrics_metrics.description: How well news organizations perform the role of holding elected officials accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among five core functions; journalists rate performance more positively than the public. Used to evaluate investigative vigor and accountability journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giving voice to underrepresented groups (core function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of news organizations' success in representing marginalized or underrepresented communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of five core functions; used to evaluate inclusivity and representational fairness in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing or correcting misinformation (core function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether news organizations adequately manage or correct misinformation as part of their core responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also discussed separately elsewhere; journalists give mixed reviews, with ~40% saying news orgs do a bad job. This evaluates editorial correction practices and fact-checking systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social media for journalistic work
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which journalists use social media in their work and the specific benefits (promoting stories, connecting with audiences, finding sources) and harms (negative impact on state of journalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: 94% use social media for work; among those, 87% say it helps promote stories, 79% say it helps connect with audiences/find sources; yet 67% say social media has a very or somewhat negative impact on the state of journalism as a whole. This dimension measures platform utility vs. systemic harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience of job-related harassment and threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequency and channels of harassment or threats directed at journalists, including the role of social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: 42% experienced job-related harassment or threats in the past year; among those, 78% say harassment came through social media at least once (implying ~33% of all journalists were harassed on social media). Used to evaluate occupational safety and risk mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom diversity and inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions of whether news organizations have sufficient gender diversity and racial/ethnic diversity, and whether addressing diversity and inclusion is a major newsroom priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: 67% say their organization has sufficient gender diversity; 32% say sufficient racial and ethnic diversity; 42% say addressing D&I is a major priority. Younger journalists are more likely to say there is insufficient diversity. This evaluates staff composition and institutional commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair treatment within organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether news organizations generally treat everyone fairly regardless of age, gender, or race/ethnicity, including disparities in perceptions across demographic groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roughly two-thirds say their organization treats everyone fairly, but Black, Hispanic, and Asian journalists are less likely than White journalists to agree. This dimension assesses workplace equity and differential experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic indicators: salaries, staffing changes, and job security
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures of journalists' recent salary changes, perceived organizational expansion or cutbacks, and concern about job security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: 41% received a salary increase in the past year, 50% say salary stayed the same, 7% experienced a pay cut; 30% say their organization has been expanding, 22% cutting back, 46% no change; 42% are at least somewhat concerned about job security. Used to evaluate economic health of the profession and organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudes toward licensing journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether people should be required to have a license to practice journalism or be free to practice without licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey finding: 74% say people should be allowed to practice journalism without needing a license, 25% favor licensing. This indicates professionalization attitudes and regulatory preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions of how much permanent change the COVID-19 pandemic has brought to news reporting at journalists' organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey findings: 26% say a great deal and 34% say a fair amount of permanent change (60% total). This metric captures structural and procedural shifts attributed to the pandemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-specific differences in newsroom conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in job satisfaction, harassment, and organizational change by the platform of the news organization (television, print, online, radio/podcasting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: TV journalists report lower emotional-well-being impacts (34% say positive) compared with online (54%), print (52%), radio/podcasting (48%); TV journalists more likely to report harassment (58%). Online outlets are the most likely to report expansion. Used to evaluate how platform origin shapes journalist experiences.
